routes.description: Establish that sufficiently early, informed, and mutually supporting historical sources preserve claims of an empty tomb and embodied appearances, and that resurrection explains this evidence better than legend, sincere mistake, or deliberate deception.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the documentary record is historically credible enough to establish the principal reported facts and the cumulative comparative inference can overcome resurrection's low prior probability by materially disfavoring the principal alternatives.

motionBridge.description: The surviving evidence must make Jesus' resurrection the strongest cumulative historical explanation of the established facts despite the event's low prior probability.

centralBridges.description: The resurrection proclamation must be traced early enough and closely enough to the original apostles to resist explanation as later legendary development.
The documentary sources must possess sufficient proximity, eyewitness connection, corroboration, and cross-checkable reliability to support their resurrection-related reports.
The reported appearances, empty tomb, claimant conduct, and transformations must jointly reduce the plausibility of sincere mistake, fabrication, and other non-resurrection explanations.
The combined likelihood of the evidence under resurrection must be strong enough to overcome an appropriately low prior and exceed the comparative support for alternatives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Internal and contextual indicators must provide defensible links between particular writings and informed or eyewitness-connected sources.
The method for crediting Christian reports must distinguish rival religious claims through consistent, case-specific historical criteria.

routes.description: Show that indirect ancient Christian reports lack the provenance, independent corroboration, examinability, and causal connection required to establish an extraordinary resurrection, while ordinary processes remain sufficient to explain the existence and sincerity of the tradition.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the surviving reports cannot independently warrant the underlying resurrection facts or meet a consistently demanding evidential threshold, leaving legend, mistake, narrative development, or deception more credible than the extraordinary conclusion.

motionBridge.description: The surviving Christian reports must remain too indirect, weakly corroborated, or insufficiently testable to establish that Jesus rose from the dead.

centralBridges.description: Strong support for an extraordinary historical claim must require reliable provenance, relevant corroboration, and a demonstrable connection between the evidence and the claimed event.
The existence and early circulation of resurrection reports must not be treated as independently establishing the death, empty tomb, appearances, or resurrection those reports describe.
Anonymity, copying, lost originals, restricted examinability, and disputed independence must materially limit what the Christian documents can establish.
Legend, sincere false belief, embellishment, or deception must remain at least as plausible as resurrection without requiring a complete reconstruction of how the tradition arose.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Sincerity, transformation, or willingness to suffer must be separated from the truth of the underlying belief because comparable commitment accompanies false beliefs.
Any evidential standard applied to the Christian reports must avoid licensing analogous supernatural claims from competing traditions without a principled distinction.

sections.title: What Counts as Strong Evidence for an Extraordinary Historical Claim
sections.rationale: This issue sets the motion's governing threshold, including whether convergent documentary testimony can overcome a low prior or whether stronger provenance, corroboration, examinability, and causal connection are required.

sections.title: Provenance, Eyewitness Access, and Early Apostolic Origin
sections.rationale: The historical force of the resurrection reports depends on whether they can be traced through informed sources to original apostolic claimants rather than merely to later communities preserving an established tradition.

sections.title: Documentary Reliability, Independence, and Corroboration
sections.rationale: The parties dispute whether internal details, cross-checkable accuracy, interlocking accounts, and asserted external support justify defeasible trust or remain compatible with dependence, embellishment, and unverified narrative construction.

sections.title: Reported Appearances, Empty Tomb, Sincerity, and Rival Explanations
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether the underlying facts are established and whether their character materially disfavors legend, perceptual error, fabrication, and sincere false belief enough to support a resurrection inference.

sections.title: Comparative Probability and Consistency Across Miracle Claims
sections.rationale: The final inference requires a consistent method for comparing resurrection with ordinary alternatives and rival religious reports, while distinguishing relative evidential superiority from sufficiency for the extraordinary conclusion.
